title: Beyond every pilgrimage
hookLine: pilgrimage, austerity and charity do not equal the Name (Sukhmani 3)

lines: A MARATHON, A FAST, A FLIGHT.
THE SAME SELF IN THE CARRY-ON.
A LONG LIST, A SHORT SENTENCE.
cards: You can run a marathon for charity, post the photos, and still be short-tempered with the person who drove you there. You can fast all day and spend it judging everyone who didn't.

You can fly across the world to a holy place and bring your worst habits in the carry-on. Big effort outside, the same old self inside. The first stanzas of the third ashtpadi are a long list of big efforts.
And they end with a short sentence.

teach.h: CHANTING, FASTING, THE FOREST, THE FIRE.
teach.b: Here's the list, from the first stanza, in paraphrase. Chanting and austerity, knowledge and every kind of meditation. Expounding the six schools of philosophy and the smritis.
Yoga, rituals and religious rites. Renouncing everything and wandering in the forest. Every kind of effort: charity, burnt offerings, gifts of jewels.
Cutting the body to pieces and offering it in the fire. Fasts and vows of every sort.
Then the short sentence: none of these equal reflecting on the Name of God. Nanak says: through the Guru, chant the Name even once. The next stanza adds the picture behind today's title.
In paraphrase: someone longs to die at a place of pilgrimage, yet pride and ego do not leave the mind.
They wash themselves day and night, and the dirt of the mind doesn't leave the body. Notice what's being measured. Not whether pilgrimage or fasting is good or bad in itself.
The stanza asks one question of every effort: does it touch the mind? Washing the body isn't washing the mind. A long journey doesn't automatically go inward.
Guru Nanak said something like it in Japji: he would bathe at the pilgrimage place, if that pleased the One; without that, what use is bathing? So the third ashtpadi isn't against effort.
It's against effort that skips the inside.
The simple, sincere thing done with the whole heart outweighs the grand thing done for show.

how: Sikhs reading Sukhmani recite these stanzas of the third ashtpadi, and Sikh teaching draws on them to stress inner remembrance and honest living over outward ritual.

o: a pilgrimage place, a sacred spot to bathe
a vow of silence kept for a season
a hermit's hut deep in the forest

games.q: the third ashtpadi's list — tap the pairs.

s: the stanza says pilgrimage and fasting are evil
it asks whether they touch the mind; none, it says, equals the Name.
the stanza pictures someone washing day and night whose mind stays dirty
the dirt of the mind doesn't leave the body.
Guru Nanak's Japji also asks what bathing at a pilgrimage place is worth without pleasing the One
without that, what use is bathing?

games.q: you've fasted, given gifts, and traveled to a holy place, but your pride came along. what does the third ashtpadi say?
o: none of these equal remembering the Name; the mind needs the washing.
games.why: pride does not leave the mind at a pilgrimage place; washing the body does not wash the mind. the Name, through the Guru, does.

practice: Pick one small thing you could do with your whole attention: make a cup of tea for someone and actually look at them as you hand it over, write two honest lines to a friend, water a plant slowly.
Picture yourself doing it with nothing extra, not for anyone to see, and let the picture settle; if you pray, say Waheguru once.

wordCard.voice: Teerath, a pilgrimage place: Sukhmani's third ashtpadi says pilgrimage, austerity, ritual and charity do not equal remembering the Name, because washing the body doesn't wash the mind.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: teerath, a pilgrimage place; the stanza says it can't wash the mind by itself.

carryVoice: Your line: simple and sincere. The short sentence outweighs the long list. Day four hundred forty-seven.
